title: Browser DevTools: Console, Network, Storage
summary: Use three DevTools panels to see what the page says, what it sends, and what it remembers, so a silent bug stops being silent.
youWillLearn: What the Console, Network and Application panels each show you
How to read a request: status code, payload and response body
How to check whether the browser really holds a login cookie
What never to paste into a chat or an issue

glossary.browser: The program Maya uses to open websites, like Chrome or Safari. It shows Notely's screens and sends her clicks on.
glossary.app server: A computer that runs the app's own code and answers the browser. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast. Notely's is Postgres, run by Supabase.
glossary.status code: A three-digit number at the start of every answer from a server that says, in short, how it went: 201 created, 404 not found, 500 server broke.
glossary.DevTools: The inspection tools built into every desktop browser. Open them with F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac.
glossary.console: The DevTools panel that shows errors, warnings and anything the page's code prints with console.log.
glossary.payload: The data the browser sent with a request, for example the note's title and body.
glossary.response body: The data the server sent back. For an error, it often contains the exact reason.
glossary.cookie: A small note the browser keeps for a website and sends back with every request to it. Logins are usually kept in one.
glossary.localStorage: A small store of names and values in the browser, per website, that any script on the page can read.
glossary.RLS: Row Level Security: database rules that decide which rows each user may read or write. Supabase relies on them to protect your tables.
glossary.cURL: A command-line tool that sends a request from the terminal, exactly as written, without a browser.
glossary.HAR file: A recording of every request in the Network panel, exported as one file. It can include cookies, tokens and response data.

steps.title: Saving a note in Notely
body: Maya writes a note in Notely and clicks Save. Her browser (the screen she types into) sends it to the app server (the computer running Notely's code), which writes it into the database (where notes live).
The answer comes back with a status code, a three-digit number that says how it went. 201 means: created.

scene.caption: Save goes from the browser to the app server, which writes the note into the database.

steps.title: The spinner that never stops
body: One day Maya clicks Save and the button shows a spinner. It keeps spinning. No red message, no crash, nothing on screen.
Something in the conversation between the browser and the app server went wrong, and the page does not say what. You cannot see it on screen. You can see it in the browser's own inspection tools.
changes: ~ Browser: Save spins forever
~ Save button works → spinning
~ Status code 201 → unknown

scene.caption: Maya clicks Save. Something goes wrong behind the screen, and the page shows nothing.

steps.title: Three panels, three questions
body: Open DevTools with F12 (Cmd+Option+I on a Mac). It has dozens of tabs, but three answer most bugs.
Console: what did the page's code say? Network: what did the page send, and what came back? Application (Storage in Firefox): what does the browser remember for this site?

callout.text: A flight recorder with three channels: the cockpit voice (Console), the radio traffic with the tower (Network), and the cargo list (Application). Each answers a different question about the same flight.

changes: + Console: what the page's code said
+ Network: every request and its answer
+ Application: what the browser remembers
~ App Server and Database fade back

scene.caption: Three DevTools panels, built into Maya's browser.

steps.title: Console: what the code said
body: The console lists errors in red, warnings in yellow, and anything the code printed. Each line links to the file and line that printed it.
Errors read the same way as in the last lesson: type, message, location. Here Maya's console has nothing red at all. That is a clue in itself: the page's code did not crash.

callout.text: A message with blocked by CORS policy means the browser refused to let your page read another site's answer. It is fixed on the server that answers, not in your page code.

changes: ~ Console: 0 errors, so nothing crashed
~ Network and Application fade back

scene.caption: The Console is empty. Whatever went wrong did not crash the page.

steps.title: Network: every request, recorded
body: The Network panel lists every request the page makes. The Fetch/XHR filter hides images and scripts and keeps only data calls. Maya's save request is there, in red.
Click it. Headers shows the address and status code. Payload shows the payload, what the page sent. Response shows the response body, what came back.

callout.text: Tick Preserve log when a bug involves a reload or a redirect, such as a login. Without it, the list is wiped on every page load.

changes: ~ Network: the save request, in red
~ App Server answered with a refusal
~ Console fades back
~ Status code unknown → 403

scene.caption: The Network panel catches the save request and the refusal that came back.

steps.title: Read the status code first
body: The first digit says which side to blame. 2xx: it worked. 4xx: the server refused what was sent: 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 wrong address, 429 too many requests.
5xx: the server itself broke, so the real error is in its logs. A row stuck on (pending) never got an answer at all.
changes: ~ Network: 403 means forbidden, the server said no

scene.caption: 403 starts with 4: the server understood the request and refused it.

steps.title: Application: what the browser keeps
body: A 403 makes you wonder: is Maya even logged in? The Application panel answers. Under Storage it lists cookies and localStorage for this site.
Notely keeps the login in a cookie named like sb-…-auth-token. It is there, so the browser holds a session. The refusal has another cause.

callout.text: Clear site data wipes cookies and storage for this site. Use it to test as a brand-new visitor, or to rule out stale data from an old version.

changes: ~ Application: the login cookie is there
~ Network fades back

scene.caption: The login cookie is present. Maya is logged in, so the 403 is about something else.

steps.title: The response body names the cause
body: Back in Network, the Response tab reads: new row violates row-level security policy for table "notes". An RLS rule only accepts notes whose user_id is the logged-in user. The insert never sent one.
Two bugs, really: the missing field, and page code that ignored a failed answer, so the spinner never stopped.

code.caption: Supabase's client does not throw on a refusal. It returns error, and your code must check it.

changes: ~ Database: its RLS rule refused the note
~ Application fades back; Network back in focus
~ Status code 403 explained: no user_id sent

scene.caption: The response body names the real cause: the database's rule refused a note with no owner.

steps.title: Copy as cURL copies your login too
body: Right-click a request and DevTools offers Copy as cURL, a cURL command that replays it from a terminal. It includes the headers: cookies, login tokens, sometimes API keys.
A HAR file export can hold the same, plus every answer. Pasted into a chat or an issue, either can hand over a working login.

callout.text: Give Claude Code the address, status code and response body, plus the Console error with its line. Remove Cookie and Authorization headers first. When it fixes a failed request, check the page also handles the failure.

changes: − Console: not part of this step
+ Shared chat: a chat or issue others can read
~ Network: copying the request copies the login

scene.caption: Copying a request copies the login cookie with it. Strip it before you share.

steps.title: Recap: look before you guess
body: Console: errors, with a link to the line. Network: every request, with status code, payload and response body. Application: cookies and storage, so you know if the user is really logged in.
A silent bug is usually a failed request nobody checked. Here the response body named the cause, and sending user_id fixed it.
changes: − Shared chat
+ Console back in DevTools
~ Save button spinning → works: user_id is sent
~ Status code 403 → 201

quiz.question: Notely's Save button spins forever. The Console is empty. What do you check next?

options.text: The Network panel: find the save request and read its status and response.
options.why: An empty Console means nothing crashed in the page. A request that failed or never answered shows up in Network, with the reason in its response body.

options.text: Reinstall the dependencies, since the Console would show any real problem.
options.why: Many failures never reach the Console, for example a refused request whose failure the code ignores.

options.text: Clear the browser cache and try again.
options.why: That may change nothing and teaches you nothing. Look at what was sent and what came back first.

quiz.question: A request to /api/summary returns 500. Where is the most useful next clue?

options.text: In the request payload, since 5xx means the browser sent bad data.
options.why: Bad input usually gets a 4xx. A 5xx means the server itself failed while handling the request.

options.text: In the Application panel, since it is probably a cookie issue.
options.why: A missing login normally comes back as 401 or 403, not 500.

options.text: In the server logs, since a 5xx means the server broke.
options.why: The browser only sees "something broke". The stack trace and real message are in the server's logs, which is the next lesson.

quiz.question: A client asks you to look into a login bug and offers to send a HAR file of their session. What is the main risk?

options.text: HAR files are too large to open.
options.why: They can be big, but size is not the danger.

options.text: It can contain their cookies and tokens, so whoever reads it can act as them.
options.why: A HAR can record full request headers and answers. Ask for an export without cookies if their browser offers one, keep it private, and delete it when you are done.

options.text: HAR files only work in the browser that made them.
options.why: Any DevTools or HAR viewer can open them. That portability is part of why leaked HAR files are dangerous.

takeaways: Console answers "what did the code say?", Network "what was sent and what came back?", Application "what does the browser remember?".
In Network, filter by Fetch/XHR, then read the status code, then the Response tab. The reason is often written there.
4xx: the server refused the request. 5xx: the server broke, so go to its logs.
Supabase's client returns error instead of throwing. Code that ignores it, or ignores a failed answer, leaves the page hanging.
Copy as cURL and HAR files can contain logins. Strip Cookie and Authorization before sharing.
